Grain-oriented electrical steel, which forms the magnetic core of transformers, is produced domestically, but U.S. output is constrained in both grade variety and total volume relative to demand. As a result, manufacturers rely on imports from Japan and South Korea, particularly for high-grade grain-oriented electrical steel. Similarly, copper conductors, on-load tap changers, bushings, and insulation materials are claimed to face high levels of import dependence. Altogether, more than 80% of U.S. demand for LPTs is currently met through imports (Bureau of Industry and Security 2021), exposing the sector to trade restrictions, tariff disputes, and global supply chain disruptions. vi This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Domestic manufacturing capacity has expanded in recent years, with facility upgrades announced by Delta Star, Hitachi Energy, and Pennsylvania Transformer and new capacity planned by Siemens Energy. Yet these expansions remain insufficient to meet rising demand from hydropower, data centers, and renewable integration. Production of the largest extra-high- voltage units remains concentrated globally, with only a handful of facilities worldwide capable of manufacturing units above 400 MVA. Hydropower rehabilitation projects in particular face additional challenges due to custom design requirements, remote locations, and regulatory needs around domestic content. Regional cost disparities driven by transportation logistics, labor markets, and import price volatility further exacerbate project risks. Regional disparities in LPT pricing highlight additional barriers. Logistics can represent 3%– 20% of transformer cost, depending on site accessibility, while labor shortages and specialized workforce retirements compound risks of project delays (U.S. Department of Energy 2024). Case studies of recent projects demonstrate how transportation of custom-engineered 100–400-ton transformers through mountain passes, waterways, and restricted bridges requires complex multimodal logistics (Office of Electricity Delivery and Energy Reliability 2014). Secondary components of pumped storage hydropower (PSH) facilities, such as turbines, hydrogenerators, and governors, add further vulnerabilities. Only a few U.S. facilities can forge large shafts or cast runners over 10 tons, and there are no domestic suppliers of hydrogenerators larger than 20 MW. Electronic control systems for excitation and protection are heavily reliant on Asian manufacturing. These gaps amplify project risks, especially as PSH deployment accelerates to support grid reliability. Recent policy measures could mitigate these supply chain challenges. The Inflation Reduction Act established, and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) modified, a domestic content bonus credit under the investment tax credit and production tax credit, which provides an additional 10 percentage points of credit value for projects that meet domestic content requirements. In May 2024, Internal Revenue Service Notice 2024-41 provided a safe harbor table for hydropower and PSH projects to help them more easily qualify for the bonus credit. To qualify, projects must ensure that all iron and steel used in applicable components are sourced from the United States and that manufactured products meet escalating domestic cost thresholds, beginning at 40% in 2024 and increasing to 55% by 2029.
